themes.consensus_view: Banks agree French borrowing costs have jumped and that worry is spreading to Italy and Greece, but they split on whether the sell-off is an overshoot to buy or the start of a wider European debt problem.

Most banks see AI spending on chips, data centers and power as the main driver of earnings and growth right now, while a smaller group worries it depends on borrowed money and revenue that has not yet caught up.

Desks repeatedly flag the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea shipping attacks as a live oil supply risk, and the one desk with a stated view expects a multi-year refill of stockpiles, but nobody else has staked a directional call.

Desks read the weak September jobs report as taking an October Fed hike off the table, with State Street and UBS expecting the next and possibly last hike in December, while Berenberg argues the market's three or four more hikes is too much.
UBS and Goldman Sachs lean positive on European stocks because company earnings are growing, while Pictet says the signs of stabilization are still mixed.
Only JPMorgan staked a view, saying traders bought the global bond selloff in record size, while the other mentions just describe the bond stress without calling a direction.
Desks describe the US job market as cooling toward slower hiring, with Western Asset calling 50,000 to 100,000 private-sector jobs a month the new normal, but nobody has staked out a contrary view.

Banks treat the November 3rd US midterms as a live policy-risk event, but only SEB stakes a view (the House likely changes hands) while William Blair says the Fed and economic growth matter far more for markets.
